name: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus

prevalence.estimate: 1-6 per 100,000 overall; up to 6% in dementia populations

ethnicAssociations: Higher recognition rates in developed countries with access to imaging

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Japanese iNPH Guidelines / International Guidelines (2005 Updated)

criteria.description: Gait disturbance: broad-based, short-stepped, magnetic gait with difficulty turning
Ventriculomegaly on imaging (Evans index >0.3) not entirely attributable to cerebral atrophy
Cognitive impairment: subcortical pattern with psychomotor slowing, impaired attention, and executive dysfunction
CSF opening pressure in normal range (70-245 mmH2O)
Clinical improvement after CSF removal (tap test or extended lumbar drainage)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Gait disturbance (required) plus ventriculomegaly, with at least one additional feature (cognitive decline or urinary symptoms). Positive response to CSF removal strongly supports diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: The classic triad of gait disturbance, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence (wet, wacky, wobbly) is present in only ~50-60% of patients. Gait disturbance is the most responsive to shunting.

pathognomonic.notes: Broad-based, short-stepped, feet appear 'glued to floor'; gait apraxia

pathognomonic.symptomName: Classic triad: gait, cognitive, urinary symptoms
pathognomonic.notes: Complete triad in only ~50-60%; gait most common and earliest
searchTerms: walking problems, thinking issues, and bladder symptoms
gait disturbance with cognitive and urinary signs
classic triad of movement, mental, and urinary problems

pathognomonic.notes: Evans index >0.3 with tight high-convexity sulci (DESH pattern); ventriculomegaly out of proportion to cortical atrophy
searchTerms: enlarged brain ventricles disproportionate to size

common.notes: Subcortical pattern: psychomotor slowing, inattention, executive dysfunction
Initially urgency; frank incontinence in later stages

occasional.notes: Bradykinesia, rigidity; can mimic Parkinson disease

laboratory: CSF opening pressure in normal range (70-245 mmH2O) on lumbar puncture
Large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test): removal of 30-50 mL CSF with gait assessment before and after
imaging: DESH (disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid-space hydrocephalus) pattern: enlarged ventricles with tight high-convexity sulci
Callosal angle <90 degrees on coronal MRI
Periventricular white matter changes (transependymal CSF migration)
Flow void sign at cerebral aqueduct on MRI
genetic: No established genetic cause for idiopathic NPH
Secondary NPH may follow SAH, meningitis, or trauma
other: Tap test (large-volume CSF removal): >10% improvement in gait speed is positive
Extended lumbar drainage (72 hours): more sensitive than single tap test
CSF infusion test: elevated resistance to CSF outflow
Gait analysis with timed up-and-go test before and after CSF removal

distinguishingFeatures: Alzheimer's has cortical cognitive pattern (amnesia, language, visuospatial)
Alzheimer's has brain atrophy proportionate to ventricular enlargement
Alzheimer's does not improve with CSF removal
Parkinson's has resting tremor, rigidity, and response to levodopa
Parkinson's gait is narrow-based with shuffling (vs broad-based in NPH)
Parkinson's does not have ventriculomegaly disproportionate to atrophy
IIH has elevated opening pressure and papilledema

redFlags: Rapidly progressive dementia should raise concern for CJD or autoimmune encephalitis rather than NPH
Prominent cortical features (aphasia, agnosia, apraxia) suggest neurodegenerative rather than NPH
Papilledema should not be present in NPH; its presence suggests alternative diagnosis
Failure to improve after adequate CSF removal questions the diagnosis
NPH and Alzheimer disease commonly coexist in elderly patients
Secondary causes (prior SAH, meningitis, surgery) should be identified as they affect prognosis
references: Relkin N, et al. Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery. 2005;57(3 Suppl):S4-16.
Nakajima M, et al. Guidelines for Management of Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (Third Edition). Neurol Med Chir (Tokyo). 2021;61(2):63-97.
Williams MA, Malm J. Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus. Continuum (Minneap Minn). 2016;22(2):579-599.
